content.title: About
content.content: Cashews are the edible seeds of the cashew tree (Anacardium occidentale), native to tropical America and now cultivated in many warm regions worldwide. Raw cashews have a delicate buttery‑nutty flavor and a crunchy texture. They are eaten raw, roasted, or used in sauces, spreads, baked goods, and plant‑based milks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cashews grow attached to a fleshy fruit called the cashew apple, not inside a hard shell like most nuts.
Raw cashews are covered with urushiol, a toxic resin, so they are always steamed or roasted before sale.
Cashew trees belong to the Anacardiaceae family, which also includes mango and pistachio.
In many African and Asian cuisines, cashews are a traditional source of plant protein.
Cashews are one of the richest dietary sources of copper, essential for bone health and nerve function.

items.title: Rich in copper
items.content: Copper supports collagen formation, immune function, and iron absorption.

items.title: Contains heart‑healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: Most of the fat in cashews is monounsaturated, which can help maintain healthy cholesterol levels.

items.title: Source of magnesium
items.content: Magnesium aids normal muscle and nerve function and participates in energy metabolism.

items.title: Provides plant protein and fiber
items.content: Cashews contribute protein and dietary fiber, promoting satiety and digestive health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin in cashews support energy metabolism.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Cashews can trigger allergic reactions, including severe anaphylaxis, in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Toxicity of raw product
items.content: Raw cashews contain urushiol, which is poisonous in large amounts; commercial cashews are always processed to remove it.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Cashews are calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: People prone to kidney stones should consume cashews in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cashews can be enjoyed as a snack, tossed into salads, oatmeal, or yogurt, blended into sauces (e.g., vegan cheese), or ground into cashew flour and butter. Choose unsalted or lightly salted varieties.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cashews in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent oil oxidation. Discard nuts that smell rancid.
